title: The Bank Guarantee Behind Imvo Zabantsundu's First Issue in 1884
dek: At 24, John Tengo Jabavu left a mission newspaper to start his own in King William's Town, with everything ready except the money.

story.event: Leaving the Lovedale mission paper and launching Imvo Zabantsundu on a bank guarantee
story.summary: In 1884 John Tengo Jabavu, whose contract as editor of the Lovedale mission's Isigidimi samaXhosa had ended, chose to start an independent newspaper in isiXhosa and English. Lacking capital, he relied on Richard Rose-Innes and the merchant James Weir, who jointly guaranteed a bank overdraft; Imvo Zabantsundu first appeared in King William's Town on 3 November 1884. When unpaid subscriptions pushed the overdraft towards four figures, the backers installed a bookkeeper and put Jabavu on a small salary, then handed the paper back to him once it was stable.
paragraphs: By 1884 John Tengo Jabavu, then 24, had come to the end of his contract as editor of Isigidimi samaXhosa, the newspaper of the Lovedale mission in the eastern Cape. He had grown up near Healdtown, the son of parents who could not read, and had learned printing in the hours before dawn while working as a teacher at Somerset East. At Lovedale he filled the paper's pages with parliamentary debates, and his political writing did not suit everyone there.

His choices, as his son later set them out, were to stay and keep his politics to himself, to go back to teaching, or to launch an independent newspaper. A friend, Meshach Pelem, wrote that staying in so restricted a post would be to bury himself alive. But a paper needed capital, and paying subscribers among a small number of readers scattered across the colony. He took a long time to decide. Meanwhile he canvassed in an election for the liberal candidate James Rose Innes and refused payment, preferring, he said, "to work for love of the cause".

Afterwards the candidate's brother, Richard Rose-Innes, found him perplexed. Jabavu had worked out the paper's name, its stance towards the parties and its mix of isiXhosa and English; he lacked only money. Rose-Innes and the merchant James Weir stood as joint guarantors with a local bank, a printing contract was signed with the Cape Mercury, and Jabavu toured the Native Territories and the Border districts, coming back confident. On 3 November 1884 the first issue of Imvo Zabantsundu appeared in King William's Town. Africans writing in the colonial press, Jabavu argued in it, had spoken out of courtesy; his readers would now "see us as we see ourselves".

Subscribers came quickly, and so did the printer's bills, while many readers never paid. When the overdraft approached four figures, the backers brought in a bookkeeper, struck off non-paying subscribers and put Jabavu on a small salary, which by Rose-Innes's account he accepted cheerfully. Once the finances were stable they handed the paper back to him. Scholars today call Imvo the first Black-owned and controlled newspaper in South Africa, and also argue that its reliance on white liberal backers later pulled it towards their politics.

quote.text: A good man will be surety for his neighbour; and he that hath lost shame will fail him. Forget not the good offices of thy surety; for he hath given his life for thee.
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira praises the man who stands surety and tells the borrower never to forget him. Imvo could not have started without its two guarantors, and gratitude is a virtue. Historians argue that the same ties later shaped what the paper would say. The story does not settle which weighs more.

reflection: Very little that matters is started entirely alone. Jabavu had the plan, the name and a sense of his readers; two other men had the credit a bank would accept. Taking their help was not a failure of independence. It was how the paper came to exist at all.

What is worth noticing is what help asks of you afterwards. When someone backs your work, with money, time or their good name, it can be wise to say plainly at the start which decisions stay yours, so that gratitude and judgement do not have to be untangled later, when both are under strain.
invitation: Think of one person whose support your work relies on, and write a single sentence about which decisions you share with them and which stay yours. Keep it somewhere you will see it.

cross_checks.claim: Jabavu edited the Lovedale mission paper Isigidimi from 1881 and left it to found his own newspaper
He canvassed for James Rose Innes in Victoria East and refused payment
Richard Rose-Innes and James Weir provided the financial backing that let the paper start
Imvo Zabantsundu first appeared in King William's Town in November 1884 (3 November), when Jabavu was 24
Imvo is regarded as the first Black-owned, independent newspaper in South Africa

research_notes: Dates: D. D. T. Jabavu (1922) says his father's Lovedale term ended in 1884 and quotes Richard Rose-Innes placing the Victoria East election in 1883; the HSRC chapter (via The Journalist) says Jabavu left at the end of his three-year contract in 1883 and canvassed in the 1884 election. The story says 'by 1884' and does not date the election. Launch date: the Press Council article quotes the first issue of 3 November 1884; some summaries give 4 November; the 1922 biography says November 1884; the story uses 3 November. 'First Black-owned': the Press Council writers (academics at UCT and UWC) call it the first Black-owned and controlled newspaper; UCT's archive and Vuk'uzenzele call it the first independent Black newspaper; SAHO's description as the first Bantu-language newspaper is contradicted by earlier mission papers such as Isigidimi itself and is not used. Ownership is not straightforward: the 1922 biography records that Weir and Rose-Innes guaranteed the overdraft, took the finances in hand during the crisis and then handed the paper back to Jabavu as proprietor, so the story describes their role rather than asserting sole ownership from the first day. The overdraft figure ('approached four figures', no currency given) and the cheerful acceptance of a small salary come from Rose-Innes's own recollection, quoted by Jabavu's son, and are attributed. Pelem's letter is paraphrased by the son, so 'bury himself alive' is not presented as a direct quotation. The two short quotations from the first issue are taken from the Press Council article. The later critique (that reliance on liberal financiers shaped the paper's politics, including the 1901 break with Weir and Rose-Innes) is stated as the view of scholars, as both the HSRC chapter and the Press Council article put it. Jabavu's later political positions (Afrikaner Bond pact of 1898, support for the 1913 Natives Land Act) fall outside this episode and are not covered. The Ben Sira passage concerns standing surety for a neighbour and is applied by analogy.
